paras: The lynching of Henry Caldwell took place early on July 30, 1882, when a masked mob took Caldwell, a Black man, from the Iron County jail at Ironton, Missouri, and hanged and shot him at a railroad bridge southeast of town. Caldwell had been bound over for trial on a charge of assaulting Mrs. Peck, a white woman of about sixty. The St. Louis wire spread the story nationally, some versions misplacing it at "Canton," while the local paper openly endorsed the killing.

Months earlier the Iron County Register had described Caldwell, a "colored denizen of Zion's Hill," as at times "out-and-out crazy" and reported his arrest and fine for carrying concealed weapons. In June the same paper called him "our colored crank" and urged the authorities to look after him.

According to the Register, at about 9:30 on the morning of Thursday, July 27, Mr. Delano of the Blue Store raised a cry for help, and C. W. Tetwiler, John Phoebe, who was Black, and others found Caldwell struggling with Mrs. Peck in her yard. Caldwell was seized after a fight and taken to Judge Dinger, who after a hearing the next day bound him over to the Circuit Court in $10,000. A St. Louis dispatch reported that threats of lynching were "freely made" at the arrest, but that it was agreed the law should take its course.

Near midnight on Saturday, July 29, thirty or forty men with masked or blackened faces gathered on Main street, swore an oath of silence, and went to the jail, posting guards at the corners of the square to keep onlookers away. They broke the inner iron door with an ax, and when Sheriff Bill Fletcher came out with a revolver, half a dozen men covered him and took the cell key. Wire reports put the mob at about a hundred and said the jailer did all he could to protect his prisoner.

With a noose already around his neck, Caldwell was run to the Iron Mountain Railroad bridge, where the rope was tied to a beam and he was thrown over the parapet. The Register said a knife slash loosened his grip on the timbers and that, because his feet touched the ground, some thirty shots were fired into him before the men dispersed. The coroner's jury found that he died at about 12:30 a.m., after being taken from the custody of the lawful authorities, hanged from the bridge and shot "by parties composing a mob."

Coroner Grandhomme summoned a jury at one o'clock, cut the body down and brought it to the Court House, and it was buried in the potter's field later that morning. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage. A week later the Register warned against a new gathering of men who had assembled to "punish" another citizen, while still calling the Caldwell lynching "not without excuse."

The Iron County Register ran its account under the headline "A Terrible Crime and its Reward," called Caldwell a "black brute," and quoted a mob member telling the sheriff "we're going to have that nigger!" It closed by saying that if any case ever called for lynch law, "this was one," and later quipped that the railroad bridge would no longer shelter "colored prowlers." The Illinois Staats-Zeitung likewise wrote that the circumstances largely excused the act, and the Register reprinted a Cincinnati Times-Star jibe about Ironton citizens choosing between church and a lynching.

Outside Missouri the story ran as a St. Louis dispatch under heads such as "Negro Lynched for Attempted Rape" and "Another Negro Lynched," and as one-line briefs in papers from Kentucky and Tennessee to Pennsylvania, Mississippi and Maryland. Several western papers printed the town as "Canton," and a condensed version filed under an Ohio heading placed it at "Canton, Ohio."

The Register counted thirty or forty men, while the wire said about a hundred. One wire version described Caldwell being shoved from the rail and mentioned no shooting, but the coroner's verdict records both hanging and gunshot wounds. The German-language Staats-Zeitung described Mrs. Peck as a seventy-year-old teacher, against the sixty given elsewhere.

A week later the Register's 'MOB LAW' editorial called the lynching 'not without excuse' while warning against further mobs.
Distant papers ran the St. Louis wire under heads such as 'Negro Lynched for Attempted Rape' and 'Another Negro Lynched'.
The Illinois Staats-Zeitung said the circumstances largely excused the act.

conflicts.note: The local paper and coroner's verdict place it at Ironton; 'Canton' is a wire garble, and the Ohio placement comes from a misfiled heading.
The local paper's figure comes from observers in town; the wire figure is round.
